The first few overs still had some contest in them. Dylan Reed gave Ridgegate a bright enough start, taking on the new ball early and making sure the innings did not begin in a crawl, but Eastmoor did get their opening reward when Edward Bell had him stumped with the score at thirty-one. That could have been the moment for the fielding side to slow the innings down. It was not, because Mason Clarke had already begun to read the surface with a clarity nobody else matched. Jacob Brown came in and played the neatest supporting hand of the early middle, four boundaries in a brisk twenty-one, enough to make sure Mason did not have to force every over himself. Their stand of forty-eight gave Ridgegate the platform, and once Jacob was taken by Steven Grant, Ryan Vale arrived and gave the innings its decisive second gear. The partnership between Mason and Ryan was the heart of the match. Ryan’s thirty-two from twenty-four was clean, direct, and sensibly paced, while Mason became more dangerous with every over, first working the ball square, then lifting through the line, then turning anything fractionally short or overpitched into boundary pressure. The eighty-six they added did more than move the total forward. It changed Eastmoor’s bowling rhythm. Timothy Lane, Ronald Stone and Paul Harris all had moments where they seemed close to dragging the rate back, yet the moment one over began to look tidy, Mason found a release shot and made the next field look defensive again. When Timothy finally bowled Ryan at one hundred and sixty-five, Eastmoor had broken the partnership but not the innings. Mason was still there, and although Brian Young later denied him a hundred by removing him for ninety-four, the damage was already deep. Mason’s innings had the right balance of violence and control: eight fours, five sixes, and enough strike management to keep the entire batting effort from turning into one-man chaos. Ridgegate’s bowling was not flawless, especially with a few expensive overs in the middle, but the wickets came at the correct moments. Taylor’s three were the most important because they removed Kevin early, Gary at the peak of the counterattack, and Paul when the tail still had a small mathematical hope. Matthew Thomas took out Edward and Jason, two of the chase’s cleaner scorers. Joseph Jackson got Steven, the one batter trying to hold the innings together. The run-outs tightened the pressure at exactly the point Eastmoor needed calm. So the result, Ridgegate by thirty-seven runs, was a fair reflection of the match’s structure. Eastmoor had enough individual blows to make the chase visible, but not enough continuity to make it truly threatening after Gary’s wicket. Ridgegate had the one innings that towered above the game, the one major partnership that changed the scale of the first innings, and enough timely bowling to stop every Eastmoor recovery just before it became dangerous. Mason Clarke was the correct player of the match because his ninety-four did not merely top-score; it defined the target, dictated the pressure, and forced Eastmoor to chase at a tempo they could only sustain in short bursts.
